messages.author: 8c6a877154df740e
messages.subject: psychophysical modelling in Stan?
parts:
Dear all,

I am trying to understand if Stan is suitable for the class of models I usually work with in computational psychophysics.

The typical model has the structure (mmh MathJax support?): 

$\log p(X | S, θ) = \sum_i \log p(x_i | s_i, θ) 
                          = \sum_i \log \int p(x_i | y_i, θ) p (y_i | s_i, θ) dy_i$

where: 
  • S is an array of known stimulus values s_i (a stimulus is usually a real scalar or 2-d real vector);
  • X is an array of recorded responses x_i (a response is usually a scalar, either integer or real-valued);
  • Y is an array of latent internal measurements y_i (an internal measurement is a real scalar or 2-d real vector) -- we are not interested in these;
  • the cardinality of S, X, Y is of the order of 10^3 trials;
  • θ is a low-to-medium dimensional parameter vector (2 to 20 parameters);
  • for simplicity, let's assume here that p(y_i | s_i, θ) is normal;
  • for simplicity, let's also assume that p(x_i | y_i, θ) = N(x_i | f(y_i, θ), σ^2(y_i, θ)), where, crucially, for many models f(y_i, θ) can be only computed via numerical integration (e.g., trapezoidal rule) of some expression involving y_i and θ.
In Matlab, I can efficiently marginalize Y away (via massively vectorized numerical integration and several computational tricks) to compute p(X | S, θ).
So far, I have been using slice sampling with moderate success, or simple MLE/MAP. However, I'd like to start using HMC -- but computing chain derivatives of parameters of dozens of different models with nested integrations quickly loses its fun.

Would Stan be able to work efficiently with this class of models?
Essentially, would it be able to handle the numerical integrations (both in terms of efficiency and autodiff?).

Thanks for your help!
Luigi

PS: Note that one numerical integration is always necessary (to obtain f(y_i, θ)).
The second integration -- to marginalize the y_i's away -- is perhaps not technically needed as I could sample from the joint posterior p(θ, Y | S, X) and then simply ignore the Y.
But this introduces a thousand or so auxiliary variables to sample from, so it's probably not the fastest thing to do -- I would probably stick to integrating each y_i away numerically (unless there are some magical gains in mixing properties).

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] psychophysical modelling in Stan?
parts:
We don't yet have a definite integrator built in yet, so
there's no way at the moment to easily implemment that
model in Stan.

But we do have a prototype that Marco Inacio built that
works with known upper/lower bounds that does the right
thing in differentiating under the integral, i.e.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Differentiation_under_the_integral_sign

That Wikipedia page also shows how to extend it to unknown
bounds (that is, how to calculate derivatives through it).

But rather than calculating that marginalization over y_i
by integrating, could you just take y to be a latent parameter
so that MCMC can do the marginalization for you?

- Bob

It'll be easy once Marco's branch is merged. Alternatively,
if you were willing to work with CmdStan or rebuild RStan,
you could work from the branch:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/tree/feature/integrate-function-parser-doc

How well it'll work will depend on the posterior geometry,
as with all HMC problems.

HMC scales well with dimension --- 1000 parameters is no big deal
so I'd definitely try that first.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] psychophysical modelling in Stan?
parts:
The question isn’t whether or not adding a bunch of auxiliary
variables is slower, it’s whether or not numerically integrating
over a 1000 dimensional space is faster than the corresponding
Monte Carlo estimate.  But Monte Carlo integration tends to do
_really_ well in high-dimensions so I think it’s worth trying a
full MCMC solution.  As Bob notes it will depend on the posterior
geometry, but doing everything at once is much easier anyways.

> PS: Note that one numerical integration is always necessary (to obtain f(y_i, θ)). 
> The second integration -- to marginalize the y_i's away -- is perhaps not technically needed as I could sample from the joint posterior p(θ, Y | S, X) and then simply ignore the Y. 
> But this introduces a thousand or so auxiliary variables to sample from, so it's probably not the fastest thing to do -- I would probably stick to integrating each y_i away numerically (unless there are some magical gains in mixing properties).

On Tuesday, 15 March 2016 20:02:18 UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
The question isn’t whether or not adding a bunch of auxiliary
variables is slower, it’s whether or not numerically integrating
over a 1000 dimensional space is faster than the corresponding
Monte Carlo estimate.
Yup. Note that integration can be extremely fast in a vectorizable language (it's 1000 separable integrals, just a big vectorized sum across a matrix).

But Monte Carlo integration tends to do
_really_ well in high-dimensions so I think it’s worth trying a
full MCMC solution.  As Bob notes it will depend on the posterior
geometry, but doing everything at once is much easier anyways.

I agree, it's worth trying.

Thanks for the answers. It's great that you already have an integration engine in the works.
For now I guess that I'll wait for its merge into the working version of Stan.
Any (vague) idea about the timeline?
